{{Short description|Data visualization}}
[[File:Mosaic-big.png|thumbnail|upright=1.2|Mosaic plot showing cross-sectional distribution through time of different musical themes in the Guardian's list of "1000 songs to hear before you die".]]
A '''mosaic plot''', '''Marimekko chart''', '''Mekko chart''', or sometimes '''percent stacked bar plot''', is a graphical visualization of data from two or more qualitative variables.<ref name="Schlotzhauer2007">{{cite book|author=Sandra D. Schlotzhauer|title=Elementary Statistics Using JMP|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5JYM1WxGDz8C&pg=PA407|date=1 April 2007|publisher=SAS Institute|isbn=978-1-59994-428-9|pages=407}}</ref> It is the multidimensional extension of '''spineplots''', which graphically display the same information for only one variable.<ref>{{cite book|title=New Techniques and Technologies for Statistics II: Proceedings of the Second Bonn Seminar|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-Pp8hbwAtq8C&pg=PA254|date=1 January 1997|publisher=IOS Press|isbn=978-90-5199-326-4|pages=254}}</ref> Although the term spineplot was originally used by Hummel<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hummel |first=Jürgen |date=1996 |title=Linked bar charts: Analysing categorical data graphically. |journal=Computational Statistics |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=23-33}}</ref> to describe univariate graphs, Cox points out that the term has also been broadly applied to displays of two or more variables.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cox |first=Nicholas J. |date=2008 |title=Speaking Stata: Spineplots and their Kin |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1536867X0800800107 |journal=The Stata Journal: Promoting communications on statistics and Stata |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=105–121 |doi=10.1177/1536867X0800800107 |issn=1536-867X}}</ref>

The mosaic plot makes it possible to visualise relationships between different categorical variables. For example,  independence is shown when the boxes across categories all have the same areas.<ref name="Friendly1991">{{cite book|author=Michael Friendly|title=SAS System for Statistical Graphics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bBIUdg5LjeUC&pg=PA512|date=1 January 1991|publisher=SAS Institute|isbn=978-1-55544-441-9|pages=512–}}</ref> Mosaic plots were introduced by Hartigan and Kleiner in 1981 and expanded on by Friendly in 1994.<ref name="Institute2013">{{cite book|author=SAS Institute|title=JMP 11 Basic Analysis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=US_pAAAAQBAJ&pg=PT251|date=6 September 2013|publisher=SAS Institute|isbn=978-1-61290-684-3|pages=251–}}</ref><ref name="FriendlyMeyer2016">{{cite book|author=Michael Friendly & David Meyer|title=Discrete Data Analysis with R: Visualization and Modeling Techniques for Categorical and Count Data|date=2016|publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC|isbn=978-1-4987-2583-5}}</ref>
Mosaic plots are also called '''Marimekko''' or '''Mekko charts''' because they resemble some [[Marimekko]] prints.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Smith |first1=Alan |title=How to apply Marimekko to data |url=https://www.ft.com/content/3ee98782-9149-11e7-a9e6-11d2f0ebb7f0 |access-date=27 September 2019 |work=Financial Times |date=6 September 2017}}</ref><ref name="mekkog">{{cite web |url=http://www.mekkographics.com/resources/charts-by-type/marimekko/ |title=Marimekko Chart |work=Mekko Graphics |access-date=13 December 2017}}</ref> 

As with [[bar chart]]s and spineplots, the area of the tiles, also known as the bin size, is proportional to the number of observations within that category.<ref name="TheusUrbanek2011">{{cite book|author1=Martin Theus|author2=Simon Urbanek|title=Interactive Graphics for Data Analysis: Principles and Examples|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xHIH1Q47FeoC&pg=PA31|date=23 March 2011|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4200-1106-7}}</ref> Although mosaic plots most commonly show the relative frequency of each combination of values, they can also be used to display the goodness with which a loglinear model fits the data.[https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vcdExtra/vignettes/a4-mosaics.html]

Mosaic plot construction is described and illustrated in detailed worked example by Jeppson and [[Heike Hofmann|Hoffman]] using the [[ggplot2]] package in the [[R (programming language)|R language]].<ref name=":0" />

== Example ==
An example of mosaic plots uses data from the passengers on the ''[[Titanic]]''. There are 2201 observations and 3 variables. The variables are:
*the gender of the person (male / female)
*the class (1st, 2nd and 3rd class, or crew)
*did this person survive the sinking (yes / no)?

{| class="wikitable"
! Gender
! Survived
! 1st Class
! 2nd Class
! 3rd Class
! Crew
|-
| rowspan="2" | Male
| No
| align="right" | 118
| align="right" | 154
| align="right" | 422
| align="right" | 670
|-
| Yes
| align="right" | 62
| align="right" | 25
| align="right" | 88
| align="right" | 192
|-
| rowspan="2" | Female
| No
| align="right" | 4
| align="right" | 13
| align="right" | 106
| align="right" | 3
|-
| Yes
| align="right" | 141
| align="right" | 93
| align="right" | 90
| align="right" | 20
|}

=== Mosaic plot construction ===
{| class="wikitable floatright"
! Order || Variable ||Axis
|-
| 1. || Gender || Vertical
|-
| 2. || Class     || Horizontal
|-
| 3. || Survived   || Vertical
|}

The categorical variables are first put in order. Then, each variable is assigned to an axis. In the table to the right, sequence and classification is presented for this data set. Another ordering will result in a different mosaic plot, i.e., the order of the variables is significant as for all multivariate plots.

At the left edge of the first variable we first plot "Gender," meaning that we divide the data vertically in two blocks: the bottom blocks corresponds to females, while the upper (much larger) one to males. One immediately sees that roughly a quarter of the passengers were female and the remaining three quarters male.

One then applies the second variable "Class" to the top edge. The four vertical columns therefore mark the four values of that variable (1st, 2nd, 3rd, and crew). These columns are of variable thickness, because column width indicates the relative proportion of the corresponding value on the population. Crew plainly represents the largest male group, whereas third-class passengers are the largest female group. The number of female crew members is also seen to have been marginal.

The last variable ("Survived") is finally applied, this time along the left edge with the result highlighted by shade: dark grey rectangles represent people that did not survive the disaster, light grey ones people that did. Women in the first class are immediately seen to have had the highest survival probability. The survival probability for females is seen to have been higher than that for men (marginalised over all classes). Similarly, a marginalization over gender identifies first-class passengers as most probable to survive. Overall, about 1/3 of all people survived (proportion of light gray areas).

[[File:Mosaic titanic independent.png]]
}}

== Properties ==
*The displayed variables are categorical or ordinal scales.
*The plot is of at least two variables. There is no upper limit, but too many variables may be confusing in graphic form.
*The number of observations is not limited, but it is not possible to read from the image, which shows relative proportions. Jeppson and Hoffman have published a modified mosaic plot that shows data density.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Jeppson |first=Haley |last2=Hofmann |first2=Heike |date=2023-02-10 |title=Generalized Mosaic Plots in the \pkg{ggplot2} Framework |url=https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2023-013 |journal=The R Journal |language=en |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=50–78 |doi=10.32614/RJ-2023-013 |issn=2073-4859|doi-access=free }}</ref>
*The areas of the rectangular tiles that are available for a combination of features are proportional to the number of observations that have this combination of features.
*The tiles can be colored according to the standardized residual from a model of independence, so that cells with excessively large or small deviations from their expected value are shaded, as in a [[heat map]], making it possible to detect possible patterns of association.
*Unlike, for example, the [[boxplot]] or [[QQ plot]], it is not possible for the mosaic plot to plot a [[confidence interval]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rice |first=Kenneth |last2=Lumley |first2=Thomas |date=2016-03-01 |title=Graphics and statistics for cardiology: comparing categorical and continuous variables |url=https://heart.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/heartjnl-2015-308104 |journal=Heart |language=en |volume=102 |issue=5 |pages=349–355 |doi=10.1136/heartjnl-2015-308104 |issn=1355-6037|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

== Criticism ==
The mosaic plot has been criticised for making the data hard to perceive and to compare visually, because the values correspond to areas.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.perceptualedge.com/example13.php |title=Design Example: Marimekko Chart |work=Perceptual Edge |access-date=30 October 2011 |last=Few |first=Stephen}}</ref><ref name="mekkog" />
